name: Serpentine
toxicityNote: Some serpentine rocks contain fibrous asbestos-type minerals; avoid dust when cutting or sanding, and do not make elixirs.
physical: Traditionally associated with a feeling of calm and balance
Crystal healers link it to circulation of energy
Folklore connects it with comfort during stress
Often kept nearby for general vitality
summary: Serpentine is a smooth, waxy green stone named for its snake-skin look, linked to grounding, kundalini awakening and gentle renewal.
intro: Serpentine is not one stone but a group of green magnesium silicates, from soft, waxy antigorite to translucent lime-green varieties, often marbled with darker veins, giving a snake-skin look. The surface can be mottled green, yellow or nearly black, and it takes a smooth, slightly greasy polish. Because it is relatively soft and carvable, it has been used for beads, bowls, statues and architectural stone for thousands of years. Pieces feel soapy and cool in the hand. Some varieties are translucent enough to glow when held to a light, like pale jade, which also leads to confusion with true jade.
history: The name likely comes from the Latin serpens, referring to the patterned surface that resembles a snake's skin, or from old beliefs that it protected against snakebite. Serpentine was carved in prehistoric times, and the Minoans of Crete used it for seals and vessels. It was used widely in medieval Europe for mortars, with the idea it would reveal poison. In California it is the state rock, and large serpentine outcrops shape unique habitats. The Maori of New Zealand carved bowenite, a hard variety, as pounamu-like ornaments. It remains a popular carving stone worldwide.
meaning: Serpentine is considered a stone of earth energy and gentle renewal. Practitioners link it with the heart and root and with the sinuous energy of kundalini, the coiled life force in yogic tradition. It is used to support grounding, steady growth and a calm approach to spiritual practice. The snake-like pattern is read as a symbol of shedding old skin, so it is used during times of change to mark the letting go of old habits. Many choose it for meditation, finding that it helps settle restless energy. It is considered a mild, friendly stone that suits those starting out with crystals, and one that pairs well with other earthy stones.
howToUse: Hold a smooth serpentine palm stone during meditation to feel grounded and unhurried. Place it near your root or lower back while lying down for a short rest. Keep a piece on your desk or windowsill to bring a calm earth presence. During a time of change, carry a small piece as a reminder to shed what no longer fits. Use it in a grid with green aventurine and clear quartz. As a carving stone, it suits bowls, spheres and figurines, which make lovely home decor.
care: Serpentine varies in hardness, but most is soft and easily scratched. A brief wipe with a damp cloth is fine, but avoid soaking, acids and cleaners, and dry it well. Cleanse by smoke, sound or selenite, and charge under the moon or in gentle morning sun. Store separately in a soft pouch away from harder stones. Some serpentine can contain fibrous minerals, so avoid creating dust when cutting or sanding, and do not make elixirs.
identify: Serpentine is usually green with a waxy, slightly greasy luster and mottled veining. It is softer than jade and can be scratched by a steel knife, whereas jade resists scratching. Many pieces sold as jade, such as new jade or Korean jade, are serpentine. Imitations include dyed stone and glass. A cool, smooth feel and cloudy translucence are typical. If a price seems too good for jade, check whether it is serpentine. Buy from sellers who label it properly.

faq.a: In crystal tradition, serpentine is a grounding stone linked with kundalini, earth energy and gentle renewal. People use it in meditation and during life changes. These are metaphysical beliefs, not medical claims.

faq.q: Is serpentine the same as jade?
faq.a: No. Serpentine is much softer and cheaper than true jade, though it can look similar. Many items sold as new jade or Korean jade are serpentine. A steel point will scratch serpentine but not jade.

A quick wipe is fine, but avoid soaking and harsh chemicals, which can dull the polish. Dry it thoroughly. Many people cleanse serpentine with smoke, sound or selenite instead, and never use it in elixirs.
